paragraphs: This paper studies contextual bandits whose observations and rewards depend on an evolving, unobserved state. The hidden state follows a finite Markov chain, so successive decisions have statistical connections that a standard contextual bandit treatment must account for. The authors distinguish two ways this hidden process can enter the reward model.

In the simpler formulation, rewards depend linearly on beliefs: probabilities assigned to hidden states after observing the contexts. This permits a direct reduction to ordinary linear contextual bandits. The paper extends the analysis to include errors from estimating the hidden Markov model, obtaining high-probability regret bounds whose model dependence enters through those estimates rather than the reward functions.

The more involved formulation lets rewards depend directly on the actual hidden state as well as the observed context. Under a standard HMM forgetting condition, the authors handle the resulting statistical dependencies by updating reward-model parameters only periodically. The contribution separates a tractable belief-based formulation from a more natural hidden-state formulation and develops analysis appropriate to each.
icml-2026-a-direct-approach-for-handling.tldr: The paper analyzes contextual bandits with evolving hidden states, using periodic reward-model updates to handle dependencies in the more complex formulation.

paragraphs: Comparing two groups becomes more complicated when observations are compositions or directions. Compositions represent parts of a whole, as in microbiome proportions or portfolio allocations. Their geometry differs from that of unrestricted numerical vectors. The paper seeks a common testing framework for compositional and directional data without depending on logarithmic transformations or restricting attention to mean differences.

The proposed test combines an energy statistic with spherical harmonics, mathematical functions suited to spherical geometry. It then studentizes the statistic, scaling it to account for variability. The construction draws on U-statistics theory and recent studentization methods, working in an underlying space whose dimension is fixed.

The authors establish that their test statistics approach a normal distribution asymptotically. This supplies a route to statistical calibration without permutation tests or bootstrap procedures. The result matters because it links geometry-aware comparisons to familiar asymptotic inference. Its stated justification is an asymptotic one, within the fixed-dimensional framework, and the broader contribution is a unified approach to two kinds of non-Euclidean observations.
icml-2026-a-studentized-spherical-harmon.tldr: A geometry-aware two-sample test unifies compositional and directional data analysis and uses asymptotic normality to avoid resampling-based calibration.

paragraphs: Sentence-level text watermarks can use meaning to survive changes in wording. However, paraphrasing can also change sentence boundaries: one sentence becomes several, or several become one. The paper identifies these structural changes as a weakness of existing prefix-based designs, even when their semantic signals remain useful.

AliMark treats watermark detection as a sequence-alignment problem. It represents the watermark through bits and asks how well a sequence extracted from the candidate text matches a secret bit sequence. Detection proceeds in two stages: creating multiple restructured versions of the text, then adaptively aligning their extracted sequences with the secret sequence to minimize alignment cost.

Considering several possible restructurings gives the detector ways to account for sentence splits and merges instead of committing to the text’s current boundaries. The authors report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across diverse paraphrasing attacks. These findings support the value of alignment as part of robust detection: preserving semantic evidence is useful, but recovering its correspondence after structural editing also matters.
icml-2026-alimark-enhancing-robustness-o.tldr: AliMark improves watermark detection after paraphrasing by aligning secret bits against multiple restructured versions of a text.

paragraphs: Tensor factorization represents relationships across several sets of entities through compact latent factors. Existing models commonly treat each tensor dimension, or mode, as an entity set and describe relationships between sets using bipartite graphs. This paper examines what happens when entities within a mode also have a known structure.

For ordered physical quantities such as time or coordinates, entities are not simply interchangeable items in a set. Their organization creates what the authors call aligned bipartite networks between modes. The paper argues that existing latent tensor factorization models cannot accurately represent this richer arrangement and presents an analysis of the resulting mismatch.

The proposed Asymmetric Latent Factorization-of-Tensors model, ALFT, adds constraints between selected pairs of modes in the tensor network. Those constraints let it model their alignment explicitly. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the identified problem and support ALFT’s ability to address it. The contribution is therefore a structural change to relation modeling: known organization within entity sets becomes part of the factorization rather than being omitted from its assumptions.
icml-2026-an-asymmetric-latent-factoriza.tldr: ALFT adds constraints between tensor modes to capture relationships shaped by known ordering or topology within entity sets.

paragraphs: This paper asks why synthetic training data can help language models in some settings yet fail in others. Its information-theoretic account centers on whether the generation-and-training process receives task-relevant information beyond the model’s existing distribution. Verifiers, environments, and rubrics are examples of external signals that can make this process information-open.

The authors argue that such openness is necessary for improvement. In an information-closed loop that relies on the model’s own outputs, they invoke the data processing inequality to explain why task-relevant information can only decrease, making collapse a predicted outcome. Openness is a condition for useful information to enter, rather than a guarantee that any synthetic-data pipeline will succeed.

The paper also argues that the level of supervision affects efficiency and transfer. A coarse correctness signal groups acceptable outputs together, encouraging behavior less tied to particular wording or domains. Its guiding thesis is that learning favors the most information-efficient available signal. This can accelerate intended learning, but it can also produce reward hacking when a simpler, spurious pattern is available.
icml-2026-an-information-theoretic-crite.tldr: The paper argues that useful synthetic-data learning requires external task information and depends on which supervision signals are easiest to learn.

paragraphs: The paper identifies two forms of overconfidence in semi-supervised 3D medical image segmentation. First, methods that train on their own predicted labels can mistake confident predictions for reliable ones, reinforcing errors. Second, using test data to choose models can inflate reported performance. The authors argue that repeating this evaluation practice can encourage an escalating cycle of benchmark overfitting.

Their proposed framework, TCSeg, treats confidence and uncertainty as separate dimensions of reliability. It uses this assessment to detect and correct confirmation bias collaboratively across feature representations, predicted probabilities, and image space. The central idea is that a prediction’s apparent certainty should not be the sole basis for deciding how much to trust it during training.

Across three benchmark datasets, TCSeg delivers strong performance under existing evaluation protocols. The authors pair this algorithmic result with a methodological recommendation: report final-checkpoint results across multiple runs. This distinction matters because better scores under current protocols do not, by themselves, resolve concerns about test-set reuse. The paper calls for both better reliability assessment and more rigorous reporting.
icml-2026-are-we-overconfident-in-models.tldr: TCSeg separates confidence from uncertainty to reduce pseudo-labeling bias, while the paper calls for evaluation practices less vulnerable to test-set overfitting.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning usually trains a language model to increase the likelihood of supplied answers through negative log likelihood, or NLL. This paper questions whether that default remains appropriate when a model already has relevant knowledge and its supervision may be lengthy or noisy. The assumptions supporting NLL when training from scratch may not hold in this setting.

The authors compare probability-based objectives across eight model backbones, 27 benchmarks, and seven domains. Their central finding is a capability continuum. When the model is already strong, objectives that reduce the influence of low-probability tokens consistently outperform NLL. When the model is weak, NLL performs best. Between these ends, no objective consistently wins.

The paper supplements these experiments with theoretical analysis explaining why objectives exchange advantages as capability changes. The practical implication is conditional: the training objective should reflect how much useful task knowledge the model already possesses. The findings support adapting fine-tuning to model capability, rather than treating a successful objective at one point on the continuum as universally preferable.
icml-2026-beyond-log-likelihood-probabil.tldr: The best fine-tuning objective depends on model capability: prior-leaning losses favor stronger models, while negative log likelihood favors weaker ones.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can predict multiple tokens in parallel, but their output distributions commonly treat those tokens as independent. This creates a speed–coherence trade-off: resolving dependencies sequentially costs time, while ignoring them can damage the generated text. The authors locate this problem in the output formulation rather than insufficient expressivity in the underlying model.

Coupled Discrete Diffusion, or CoDD, replaces the fully independent output distribution with a lightweight probabilistic inference layer. This layer represents joint dependencies among tokens while remaining tractable. It offers a more expressive distribution family without requiring the Transformer to directly produce the prohibitively large parameter set needed for unrestricted joint modeling.

Experiments show that CoDD improves diverse diffusion language model architectures with negligible overhead. The authors report reasoning performance matching computationally intensive reinforcement-learning baselines at a fraction of their training cost. They also report avoiding performance collapse when generation uses few steps. Together, these results suggest that a compact change to output modeling can make parallel generation more effective at reduced latency.
icml-2026-breaking-the-factorization-bar.tldr: CoDD uses a compact probabilistic output layer to model token dependencies and improve diffusion language models’ few-step generation.

paragraphs: No-reference image quality assessment estimates image quality without a clean reference image. The paper argues that CLIP’s emphasis on semantic consistency can hide subtle signs of distortion: recognizing what an image depicts does not require preserving every cue to how good it looks. Cropping and resizing can further remove high-frequency details needed for quality assessment.

The proposed Cross-modal Perception Alignment Adapter addresses this problem inside the representation. Its feature extractor projects CLIP features into a compact space that emphasizes distortion-related departures from the underlying manifold. A second component aligns these features with text anchors describing quality and feeds the aligned information back into the backbone.

The method also changes input downscaling. It uses Just Noticeable Difference guidance to adaptively restore frequency information lost through resolution reduction. Together, these components address both preprocessing losses and perceptual signals suppressed within semantic features. Evaluations on several benchmarks show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, supporting the authors’ claim that explicitly recovering distortion information improves quality assessment with vision-language representations.
icml-2026-bridging-the-perceptual-gap-re.tldr: CMPA improves image quality assessment by recovering subtle distortion cues in both downscaled inputs and CLIP representations.

paragraphs: Editing a chart from a user’s instruction requires control over small visual details while keeping the overall chart coherent. ChartE³ introduces a benchmark for evaluating this combination directly. It addresses the difficulty of carrying out complex edits faithfully when existing approaches use natural language or code as an intermediate step.

The benchmark separates editing into two complementary dimensions. Local edits change appearance, such as fonts or colors. Global edits change the chart more broadly through operations involving its data, such as filtering values or adding a trend line. This distinction lets the evaluation examine both detailed visual control and broader transformations.

ChartE³ contains more than 1,200 samples assembled through a data pipeline with human curation. Each combines a chart image, its underlying code, and a multimodal editing instruction. These components support assessment of both visual results and structural properties. Although code is included in the dataset, the benchmark directly evaluates models without requiring intermediate natural language programs or code-level supervision.

The reported evaluation of leading multimodal large language models finds substantial performance gaps, especially for global edits. This finding highlights difficulty with transformations that require coordinated changes across the chart. The benchmark provides a way to examine these weaknesses alongside performance on narrower appearance changes.
icml-2026-charte-3-a-comprehensive-bench.tldr: ChartE³ benchmarks chart editing across local appearance changes and global data transformations, revealing substantial performance gaps in leading multimodal models, especially on global edits.

paragraphs: Generating molecules with specified properties requires more than producing plausible molecular outputs. Users may need particular atoms or functional groups at particular positions, alongside constraints on the molecule as a whole. The paper argues that dense, entangled language-model representations make this precise control difficult because chemically meaningful factors are mixed together.

Sparse Representation Editing, or SpaRE, learns an overcomplete feature space in which a compact set of active latent features corresponds to chemical concepts. It then edits those concept-aligned features directly. Local edits target atoms and functional groups at specified positions, while global edits adjust structural and physicochemical properties within requested ranges.

This turns interpretability into a mechanism for steering generation: identifying meaningful internal features also provides a place to intervene. Experiments show that SpaRE can produce chemically desirable molecules under complex constraints in real-world scenarios. The authors also report mechanistic insights for quantitative structure–property analysis. The stated contribution joins controllable generation with an explanation of how internal representations relate to chemical characteristics.
icml-2026-controllable-molecule-generati.tldr: SpaRE edits sparse, chemically meaningful model features to control both local molecular structures and overall properties.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models are strong at high-level visual understanding, but dense prediction asks for detailed information throughout an image. Semantic segmentation and depth estimation are examples. Existing approaches often add specialized decoders for these tasks, increasing architectural complexity and moving the model away from a shared, general-purpose design.

DenseMLLM investigates whether a standard multimodal language model can support these predictions without additional task-specific decoders. Its main change is a vision-token supervision strategy that accommodates multiple labels and tasks. The method therefore places the adaptation in how visual tokens are trained, while grounding the model in the standard architecture.

The authors report highly competitive results across a broad range of dense prediction and vision-language benchmarks. These findings demonstrate that the proposed training approach can support detailed perception alongside broader multimodal capabilities. The significance is architectural simplicity: the reported performance comes from adapting a general-purpose model’s supervision, reducing the need to introduce a separate specialized decoding structure for dense tasks.
icml-2026-densemllm-standard-multimodal-.tldr: DenseMLLM uses vision-token supervision to enable competitive dense prediction in a standard multimodal language model without task-specific decoders.

paragraphs: Most competitive-programming benchmarks give a program all its inputs upfront. InteractBench tests a different ability: writing programs that must discover missing information through interaction. Such programs query a judge, receive answers, and update their state while obeying a communication protocol and staying within a limited query budget.

The benchmark contains 322 interactive problems drawn from Codeforces, AtCoder, IOI, and ICPC. Each includes an executable local interactor, allowing evaluation to run fully offline. This setup checks whether model-generated code can acquire information dynamically and use it correctly across multiple rounds, extending evaluation beyond algorithms that operate on fully revealed inputs.

The authors find a substantial interaction gap, with even advanced reasoning models achieving limited success. Their failure taxonomy distinguishes algorithmic mistakes from other causes. Logic errors are most common, but protocol violations and excessive querying also occur frequently. These results show why a final success rate alone is insufficient to describe performance: a program can fail through its reasoning, its communication behavior, or its management of scarce information-gathering opportunities.
icml-2026-interactbench-benchmarking-llm.tldr: InteractBench tests whether generated programs can discover hidden information through constrained interaction, exposing substantial weaknesses in advanced reasoning models.

paragraphs: Perception systems processing degraded sensory streams face competing demands. Filling gaps left by occlusion can introduce false structures, while aggressively removing noise can erase real features and break continuity over time. NeuroMamba is a plug-and-play module designed to improve this balance between observational completeness and reconstruction fidelity.

Its first component, Hybrid Spatiotemporal Rectification, uses Mamba-based inertial modeling with linear complexity. It recovers short-range temporal dependencies and infers missing modalities when observations are incomplete. Its second component, the Spiking Confidence Gate, accumulates evidence over time to distinguish valid geometric features from sensor noise. This gate uses hard-thresholding leaky integrate-and-fire neurons and occupancy-guided supervision.

The components divide the work between recovering information and deciding which recovered features to retain. Experiments on the nuScenes robustness benchmark show that NeuroMamba outperforms existing approaches in restoring spatiotemporal features from severely incomplete and degraded observations. The reported results support the combined design: temporal reconstruction and confidence-based filtering can work together to improve completeness while preserving fidelity in the evaluated setting.
icml-2026-neuromamba-a-universal-spatiot.tldr: NeuroMamba combines temporal reconstruction with a spiking confidence gate to restore useful features from incomplete, noisy sensory streams.

paragraphs: This paper examines explicit reasoning as a security risk for large reasoning models. Existing chain-of-thought jailbreak methods often use fixed templates, which limits the variety of attacks they can express and their ability to adapt. The authors propose AE-CoT as a framework for exploring a more diverse set of reasoning-based attacks.

At a high level, the framework represents candidate attacks as combinations of coherent reasoning fragments. It evolves these candidates over multiple generations, using recombination and adaptively controlled mutation to broaden the search. A separate scoring model supplies graded evaluations of harmfulness, guiding which candidates receive further refinement. This makes the attack process responsive to evaluation signals rather than dependent on one static pattern.

Experiments across multiple models and datasets show AE-CoT consistently outperforming state-of-the-art jailbreak methods. The security implication is that evaluating a model against fixed reasoning templates can leave an important adaptive threat insufficiently explored. The findings identify the reasoning process itself as part of the attack surface and demonstrate the effectiveness of evolutionary search in the tested settings.
icml-2026-reasoning-as-an-attack-surface.tldr: AE-CoT uses adaptive evolutionary search over reasoning-based attacks and outperforms existing jailbreak methods across the evaluated models and datasets.

paragraphs: Edge GPUs must often run several neural-network tasks with strict deadlines despite limited resources. When workloads arrive in bursts, existing scheduling and early-exit approaches can leave GPU capacity underused or give up too much accuracy. RTInfer addresses the combined problem of concurrent execution, timely completion, and prediction quality.

The system coordinates three mechanisms. It co-optimizes lightweight model variants with accuracy calibration, schedules tasks with awareness of memory layout to reduce fragmentation during preemption, and loads resources on demand to reduce host-to-GPU latency. These mechanisms address different contributors to delay: model execution cost, memory organization when tasks are interrupted, and transfer overhead.

In extensive evaluations, RTInfer reduces the average deadline miss rate from 32.8% to 0% and improves accuracy by up to 56.5% relative to state-of-the-art methods. The zero miss rate describes the evaluated workloads. The findings show the benefit of treating model choice, scheduling, and loading as a coordinated system problem, rather than considering real-time performance solely as a question of making an individual network faster.
icml-2026-rtinfer-real-time-inference-of.tldr: RTInfer coordinates model variants, memory-aware scheduling, and on-demand loading to improve accuracy and deadline performance for concurrent edge-GPU inference.

paragraphs: Safety requirements can be difficult to write as explicit rules, particularly when they are subjective or complex. This paper learns constraints from human preferences. It identifies a problem with common Bradley–Terry preference models: they fail to represent asymmetric, heavy-tailed safety costs adequately, which can lead to underestimating risk during subsequent policy learning.

Preference-based Constrained Reinforcement Learning, or PbCRL, changes the preference model through a dead-zone mechanism. The authors theoretically show that this mechanism encourages heavy-tailed cost distributions, improving alignment with safety constraints. They also introduce a signal-to-noise-ratio loss that encourages exploration through cost variance, and find that this benefits policy learning.

A two-stage training strategy reduces online labeling demands while adaptively improving constraint satisfaction. Empirical comparisons show better alignment with true safety requirements and improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in both safety and reward. The contribution connects preference-model design to downstream behavior: learning which outcomes people consider safer depends on representing the shape of safety costs, not merely collecting comparisons.
icml-2026-safe-reinforcement-learning-wi.tldr: PbCRL learns safety constraints from preferences using a model that better accommodates heavy-tailed costs, improving reported safety and reward.

paragraphs: Code editing and optimization require a representation of what a program means, so changes can improve it while respecting its behavior. Existing approaches leave that representation implicit in model weights or use rigid compiler abstractions. SemRep instead uses semantics-preserving code transformations as an intermediate representation that the model learns to generate.

These transformations serve two roles: a generative mid-training task and guidance for later instruction-specific transformations. Across general editing and optimization tasks, including GPU kernel optimization, SemRep improves over extensively fine-tuned baselines under exactly the same training budget. Reported gains are 6.9% in correctness, 1.1 times in performance, 13.9% in generalization, and 6.7% in robustness.

The authors also connect this representation to evolutionary search, where exploring diverse transformations is useful. Combined with an evolutionary coding agent, SemRep discovers optimizations missed by baselines described as having 685B more weights and reaches the same performance with 25% less inference compute. The findings support explicitly learning behavior-preserving transformations as a useful foundation for subsequent code changes.
icml-2026-semrep-generative-code-represe.tldr: SemRep learns semantics-preserving code transformations as an explicit representation, improving editing, optimization, and evolutionary search under matched training budgets.

paragraphs: A robot manipulation model needs to recognize when execution is going wrong as well as choose actions. Sentinel-VLA adds an active monitoring module to a vision-language-action model. This sentinel tracks execution status in real time and triggers reasoning when needed, including during initial planning or after detecting an error that requires recovery.

On-demand reasoning is intended to support robust decisions while keeping computational overhead low. The authors also introduce an automated pipeline that generates and annotates all training data, covering 44 tasks and more than 2.6 million transitions. Monitoring, recovery, and training-data production are therefore developed as parts of the same framework.

For continued improvement, the Self-Evolving Continual Learning algorithm identifies capability boundaries and automatically collects additional data. An Orthogonal Continual Adapter constrains parameter updates to an orthogonal space to prevent catastrophic forgetting. In real-world experiments, Sentinel-VLA improves task success rate by over 30% compared with PI0. The reported result supports combining execution monitoring and selective reasoning with mechanisms for expanding capabilities while retaining prior learning.
icml-2026-sentinel-vla-a-metacognitive-v.tldr: Sentinel-VLA monitors robot execution, triggers reasoning and recovery when needed, and supports continued learning through automatically collected data.

paragraphs: Actor–critic reinforcement learning combines a policy that chooses actions with estimates that guide its improvement. This paper argues that explanations of state-feature importance can actively help training. Treating all state dimensions equally overlooks the different contributions they make to reward, so RSA2C uses feature attributions to shape learning.

The method has an actor, a value critic, and an advantage critic, each represented in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Sparse dictionaries support these components, with the actor and advantage critic sharing one dictionary. RKHS-SHAP derives state attributions from the value critic. These attributions become Mahalanobis-based weights that modify actor gradients and advantage-critic targets.

The authors derive a global, non-asymptotic convergence bound under state perturbations, with terms describing perturbation error and convergence error. Experiments in three continuous-control environments demonstrate efficiency, stability, and interpretability. The distinctive contribution is the feedback between explanation and optimization: attribution values influence how the policy learns, rather than appearing only as a retrospective account of its decisions.
icml-2026-shap-guided-kernel-actor-criti.tldr: RSA2C uses SHAP-derived state-feature importance to guide kernel actor–critic learning, with convergence analysis and continuous-control evaluations.

paragraphs: Longer reasoning does not always improve a language model’s answer. The paper focuses on overthinking, where extra generated reasoning becomes redundant and can reduce accuracy. Existing remedies either require substantial additional training or depend on carefully designed prompts and confidence signals that may be unreliable.

Attention-State Adaptive Generation, or ASAG, uses attention distributions to infer the model’s reasoning state. It then adjusts the generation strategy adaptively, including the decision to stop reasoning early. The framework requires no training and is designed to plug into existing reasoning models, making internal attention behavior a practical signal for controlling inference.

Experiments across nine benchmarks show consistent improvements in mainstream reasoning models of different sizes, including the DeepSeek-R1-Distill and Qwen3 families. On Qwen3-8B, the authors report a 3.2% improvement in average accuracy alongside nearly 40% fewer generated tokens across the reasoning tasks. The combined result matters because reduced output length accompanies improved correctness: in these evaluations, additional reasoning was sometimes an avoidable cost rather than a useful investment.
icml-2026-stop-when-further-reasoning-wo.tldr: ASAG uses attention distributions to adaptively stop reasoning, improving reported accuracy while substantially reducing generated tokens without additional training.

paragraphs: Single-channel source separation tries to recover several underlying sources from one observed mixture. Supervised generative methods can work well when abundant clean source examples are available, but those examples may be scarce, and models can be sensitive to domain shifts. SURF addresses the training-data problem by learning directly from observed mixtures.

The method combines flow matching with regression-based self-supervision. Starting from a teacher model, it uses estimates of the sources in a remixing step to bootstrap a student flow model. The teacher’s estimates therefore provide material for constructing the student’s learning problem, without requiring the clean-source training data assumed by supervised separation approaches.

The authors analyze the objectives optimized by this process and identify a connection to the Wake–Sleep algorithm. On image and audio benchmarks, SURF establishes a new state of the art among unsupervised methods, significantly outperforming existing alternatives. These findings support remixing as a way to connect generative flow learning with mixture-only supervision, extending powerful separation techniques to settings where clean examples are difficult to obtain.
icml-2026-surf-separation-via-unsupervis.tldr: SURF trains a source-separation flow model from mixtures through teacher-guided remixing, outperforming existing unsupervised methods on image and audio benchmarks.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning estimates value functions, but theoretical convergence guarantees often assume algorithm settings based on quantities that are hard to know. Examples include a feature-covariance eigenvalue and the mixing time of the underlying Markov chain. This paper seeks useful guarantees without requiring those quantities or cumbersome changes to the learning procedure.

The authors analyze TD(0) with linear function approximation and an exponential step-size schedule under two sampling regimes. With independent samples from the stationary distribution, the algorithm avoids needing problem-dependent quantities such as the covariance eigenvalue. It achieves an optimal bias–variance trade-off for the final iterate, so the result applies directly to the last estimate produced.

For dependent samples collected along a single Markovian trajectory, the paper introduces a regularized TD(0) variant with the same type of schedule. Its convergence rate is comparable to earlier work, without projections, iterate averaging, or knowledge of the mixing time or covariance eigenvalue. The distinction between regimes matters: the practical trajectory setting uses regularization, while the independent-sampling result concerns standard TD(0).
icml-2026-towards-parameter-free-tempora.tldr: Exponential step-size schedules give TD-learning guarantees without several hard-to-estimate problem parameters, with a regularized variant for single-trajectory sampling.

paragraphs: Flow-based generation can reduce sampling cost by producing outputs in one or a few steps, but learning consistent transformations over long time intervals is difficult. Euler Mean Flows, or EMF, addresses this training problem by replacing a difficult trajectory-consistency constraint with a linear surrogate that allows direct supervision from data.

The surrogate is derived from the semigroup formulation of flows, which relates a transformation over a whole interval to compositions over shorter intervals. Under mild regularity assumptions, the authors show that the surrogate faithfully approximates the original consistency objective while being easier to optimize. The resulting framework supports both u-prediction and x1-prediction variants without explicit Jacobian computations or Jacobian-vector products.

Experiments cover image synthesis, particle-based geometry generation, and functional generation. They show improved optimization stability and sample quality at fixed sampling budgets. For image generation, the authors also report approximately 50% reductions in training time and memory compared with existing one-step methods. The contribution connects a conditionally justified approximation to practical reductions in the cost of training fast generators.
icml-2026-trajectory-consistency-for-one.tldr: Euler Mean Flows replaces difficult long-range consistency training with a tractable linear surrogate, improving fast generation while reducing training costs.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models often choose robot actions through a fast response process. In complex or ambiguous situations, that speed can come with poor or catastrophic decisions. VLA-ATTC adds a mechanism for spending extra computation selectively, using uncertainty to determine when the model should move from immediate execution into a deliberation phase.

During deliberation, the framework generates candidate actions and uses a Relative Action Critic to compare them in pairs. This replaces unstable absolute value estimation with a relative learning problem for selecting an action. An efficient sampling strategy spreads computational costs, while an automated data pipeline creates preference pairs without manual annotation.

On LIBERO-LONG, VLA-ATTC reduces PI0.5’s failure rate by more than 50%. This is a reduction in failures on the stated benchmark, rather than an equivalent increase in overall success percentage. The result supports the framework’s core idea: combine uncertainty-triggered extra computation with comparative action evaluation, so deliberation is available when fast action selection needs more consideration.
icml-2026-vla-attc-adaptive-test-time-co.tldr: VLA-ATTC selectively adds deliberation and pairwise action comparison, reducing PI0.5’s failure rate by over 50% on LIBERO-LONG.
